claims.text: The proposed framework independently computes lattice and electronic heat transport.
The framework combines DFT-derived elastic and vibrational calculations with machine-learning-enhanced electron–phonon coupling models.
The framework will predict the total thermal conductivity of high-purity, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K within 10% of experiment.
The target material is a defect-free HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy with oxygen below 1 wt.%.
Low-impurity HfNbTaTiZr is representative of typical refractory-alloy experiments.
Atomic-scale disorder and variations in atomic mass and force constants influence phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Electronic-band-structure features affect electron–phonon interactions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Temperature-dependent DFT-derived elastic and vibrational calculations can incorporate anharmonic phonon scattering to compute lattice conductivity.
Machine-learning-enhanced electron–phonon coupling models can independently estimate electronic thermal conductivity and capture complex band interactions.
Computing lattice and electronic transport through separate routes prevents conflation of the two contributions.
The framework will correctly partition total thermal conductivity into lattice and electronic components.
The framework will provide an approximately 10–15% relative accuracy gain over earlier methods.
Earlier analytical or combined models have errors above 10–15% for HfNbTaTiZr thermal conductivity.
A major source of error in earlier HfNbTaTiZr models is conflation of lattice and electronic transport.
The framework is reliable primarily from 300 to 1200 K for high-purity samples with minimal non-intrinsic scattering centers.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic contributions become comparable in HfNbTaTiZr.
Comparable lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K make channel separation more difficult and can increase prediction errors beyond 10%.

Time-domain thermoreflectance and electrical measurements interpreted with the Wiedemann–Franz law can provide experimentally separated lattice and electronic conductivity estimates for the proposed test.
Deviation exceeding 10% in total conductivity or either separated contribution, or failure to reproduce their temperature dependences, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
